attribution.note: Zitron's own words on his newsletter, stated as his own view.

semantics.note: Faithful. He contrasts robots acting on their own accord with remote human control. The event setting is clear from context, and the claim about media credulity is rightly left out.

contract.note: His own words mention walking as well as doing things, so assessing walking separately from interactions is a fair, ordinary reading. Treating partial teleoperation as a mixed result follows from his blanket wording.

evidence.note: Ars Technica, Oct 15, 2024: reports an analyst note on tele-ops, an Optimus unit on video saying a human was assisting it, and conversations that pointed to human operators.

Same article: Bloomberg sources and an engineer quoted by Scoble say the robots walked without external control, using AI. This goes against the blanket remote-control account as far as walking is concerned.

reviews.rationale: Credible reporting says humans remotely controlled the guest interactions, including speech, so that part holds. The same reporting says walking was AI-controlled without outside input, which contradicts his blanket claim that what was shown was remotely operated rather than robots walking on their own.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Captures both parts: that Altman continually lies about progress toward superintelligence, and that the media does not question him. Leaving out the general remark about failure and deceit is acceptable.

contract.note: Reading lying as knowing misrepresentation and the media charge as a broad pattern of weak scrutiny is ordinary and fair. Limiting the claim to progress toward superintelligence matches his words.

evidence.note: Altman's own essay, the one Zitron refers to. It hedges the timeline. It shows what Altman said, not whether he knew it was false.
Ars Technica questioned the 'few thousand days' forecast and pointed to Altman's incentives. This is partial counterevidence to the media charge, but one article cannot establish the overall pattern.
Toner's allegations, which are disputed, concern the board and safety processes, not public claims about progress toward superintelligence.
TIME covered the allegations that Altman lied. This is some media scrutiny of his truthfulness, but not a representative sample.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet shows multiple knowingly false statements by Altman about progress toward superintelligence. The dishonesty allegations concern governance and are disputed. Some outlets did scrutinize him, but the packet has no representative sample of coverage. Neither part is settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Mostly faithful, but it softens 'lacks any' mass-market product-market fit to 'lacks'. Leaving out the media-faith remark is acceptable. 'Horrible business' is an evaluation and cannot be checked.

contract.note: Taking the product as ChatGPT and product-market fit as substantial sustained demand is an ordinary reading. Requiring realized quarterly operating cash flow for 'burns money' is strict, but the result turns on the product-market-fit part either way.

evidence.note: A projected full-year 2024 loss, not a realized cash-flow figure for the quarter. Under the contract it is context, though it is consistent with heavy spending.
Company-confirmed, Aug 29, 2024: more than 200 million weekly ChatGPT users, double the figure from the previous November. This is evidence of broad, sustained demand. It is a company disclosure.
Company statement, Sept 5, 2024: more than 1 million paid business seats, up from 600,000 in April. This shows people are willing to pay. It is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: During Q3 2024, ChatGPT had more than 200 million weekly users, double the figure from under a year earlier, and paid business seats were growing fast. That is substantial sustained mass-market demand, which contradicts his claim that it 'lacks any' product-market fit. The money-burning part is unresolved because the packet has only a projected loss figure. 'Horrible business' is an evaluation and is not scored.
